newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major demands end to EU beef ban.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major demands end to EU beef ban.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major renewed his demand on Tuesday for an end to the European Union's ban on British beef exports and dropped a hint he would sack his farm minister if he wins the May 1 election.

Major, keen to portray his Conservative party as a staunch defender of the national interest, also called on Britain's European partners to put their own house in order by raising their meat hygiene standards to British levels.

The prime minister came to the market town of Tavistock in western England to soothe farmers bruised by the year-old crisis over mad cow disease to find that Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg was still the target of their fury.
Several farmers who packed into the town's cattle market told Major they wanted Hogg's head as a price for staying loyal to the Conservatives at the election.

"I made it quite clear that a lot of farmers have lost confidence in the ministry team, and in one person in particular. I didn't name him, but everyone knew I was talking about Mr Hogg," Ian Pettyfer, chairman of the Devon branch of the powerful National Farmers' Union, told reporters after meeting Major.
"The prime minister made it clear he would start afresh with a new team and adopt a hands-on approach to the agriculture ministry," Pettyfer added.

Major defended his government's handling of the mad cow crisis, which erupted in March 1996 when the European Union slapped a worldwide ban on British beef after scientists discovered evidence that a fatal brain-wasting disease could be transmitted to humans from cattle.

He said the crisis, which has so far cost British taxpayers 3.5 billion pounds ($5.7 billion), was not the fault of farmers but "the result of market panic and in some cases political panic in countries right the way across Europe".

Major called on the EU to start lifting the beef ban now that Britain was slaughtering cattle most at risk of carrying the disease and had tightened its hygiene checks on meat, which he said were now the toughest in Europe.
Turning the tables on Britain's health-conscious EU partners, Major said: "What we are saying to the Europeans is that we have put our house neatly in order.

"So firstly, begin to lift the ban on British beef and, secondly, since you have felt so strongly about us putting our house in order, isn't it about time that you put your own house in order?" Major told the farmers to loud applause.
Hogg's fumbling performance in the past year was the talk of the market.

"Having him removed would be the best job. Put somebody in his place who fully understands agriculture," said Ruth Burrow, a local dairy farmer who was wearing a shirt saying "This cow's not mad, she's bloody livid!".
Another farmer, John Dawe, said: "If we think that the minister of agriculture is staying, we will not vote Conservative."
But Major was well received at the cattle market and in the town itself when he plunged into the crowd to shake hands with wellwishers.
Another local farmer, Garry Hoare, said he would be sticking with the Conservatives despite the mad cow crisis. "I don't think any other government could have done any better," he said.
